Please read /papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/research-progress/handoffs/06_MC08_MANUSCRIPT_AND_NEXT_SESSION_20261102.md. We are going to continue brainstorming the best path forward for **[B] MC08-B03 — Astra:** explore a source-dependent energy-response relation that could supply the missing signed bound.

Please include the notes here within the new 01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/brainstorm folder. Include chat histories in the chat-histories folder as usual.

First, I'd really like to understand the energy picture better. Can you summarize it based on the recently written manuscript? Don't focus yet on the outstanding problem, just on how to define energy for different Fock states in this Hilbert space, and also on the transfer operator and how that plays into the current picture.
I’ll read the handoff and manuscript, then explain the Fock-state energies and the transfer operator. I’ll also save the discussion notes and register this chat in the new brainstorm folder.

The manuscript has two distinct energy descriptions: the theta spectrum \(E_m=\pi m^2\), and the Hamiltonian constructed from the coefficient-transfer dynamics. I’m keeping their state labels separate so the explanation makes clear which Fock states have definite energies in each description.

A useful detail emerges from the transfer Hamiltonian: an occupation pattern such as “sites 1 and 3 occupied” generally has no definite energy. In the manuscript’s real coefficient basis, these occupation states have zero mean Hamiltonian energy, while suitable superpositions can have nonzero energy. I’ll include a two-mode example to make that distinction concrete.

The explanation now connects the square-energy levels to the filtered theta source, then to the coefficients and their fermionic transfer amplitudes. I’m saving it in the new brainstorm folder and linking it from the MC08 register. The note stays focused on this energy picture, with the signed-bound discussion left for our next step.

**Energy comes from a chosen Hamiltonian; the Fock-space construction alone does not assign it.** The [manuscript](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/manuscript/main.tex) contains two distinct Hamiltonians: one describes the theta source’s energy levels, and the other generates the coherent part of the coefficient-transfer dynamics.

For a one-particle space \(\mathfrak h\), the fermionic Fock space is
\[
\mathcal F_-(\mathfrak h)
=\mathbb C\Omega\oplus\mathfrak h\oplus\wedge^2\mathfrak h\oplus\cdots.
\]
It contains the vacuum, one-particle states, two-particle states, and so on. Antisymmetry permits at most one fermion in each mode.

If the one-particle Hamiltonian has eigenmodes with energies \(\epsilon_m\), its noninteracting Fock Hamiltonian adds their energies:
\[
\mathbb H=\sum_m\epsilon_m b_m^\dagger b_m,
\qquad
E_{\{m_1,\ldots,m_r\}}=\epsilon_{m_1}+\cdots+\epsilon_{m_r}.
\]
An occupation state has a definite energy **when its occupied modes are energy eigenmodes**. Otherwise, it generally has an energy distribution.

For the theta source, those eigenmodes are particularly concrete. On the circle,
\[
L=-\pi\partial_x^2,\qquad
L e^{imx}=\pi m^2 e^{imx}.
\]
Using the positive modes \(m\ge1\), the energies are \(\pi,4\pi,9\pi,\ldots\). The corresponding Fock Hamiltonian is
\[
\mathbb H_\theta=\sum_{m\ge1}\pi m^2 b_m^\dagger b_m.
\]

| Occupied energy modes | Total energy |
|---|---:|
| Vacuum | \(0\) |
| \(1\) | \(\pi\) |
| \(2\) | \(4\pi\) |
| \(1,2\) | \(5\pi\) |
| \(1,3\) | \(10\pi\) |
| \(1,2,3\) | \(14\pi\) |

Thus two states with the same particle number can have different energies. A superposition of different-energy states has mean energy equal to the probability-weighted average of those energies.

The theta primitive uses the **one-particle thermal trace**
\[
Q(\beta)=\sum_{m\ge1}e^{-\beta E_m},
\qquad
p(u)=e^uQ(e^{4u}),\qquad \beta=e^{4u}.
\]
This is the square-spectrum sum in the [defining theta series](https://dlmf.nist.gov/20.2.E3). In full-circle notation, \(Q=\tfrac12(\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta L}-1)\): remove the zero mode and the double counting of \(+m,-m\).

Although we can construct all the many-fermion states above, the primitive uses the one-particle sector. The full fermionic partition function would instead be
\[
\Xi(\beta,z)=\prod_{m\ge1}(1+ze^{-\beta E_m}),
\]
with \(Q(\beta)\) as its coefficient of \(z\).

The source \(\Phi\) further weights each energy level:
\[
\Phi(u)=e^u\sum_{m\ge1}
P_0(\beta E_m)e^{-\beta E_m},
\qquad P_0(x)=2x^2-3x.
\]
For \(u\ge0\), these weights are positive. After normalization, they define a **filtered thermal mixture**. Changing \(u\) changes the temperature and the filter; the underlying energies \(\pi m^2\) stay fixed.

The coefficient transfer uses a different one-particle basis, the sites \(\lvert j\rangle_c\) of \(\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)\). These labels count coefficient positions. In particular, \(\lvert0\rangle_c\) is a one-particle state; it is distinct from the Fock vacuum \(\Omega\).

The source supplies
\[
c_n=\frac1{(2n)!}\int_0^\infty u^{2n}\Phi(u)\,du,
\qquad F(w)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nw^n.
\]
Each coefficient incorporates the complete energy spectrum. The transfer is
\[
K_v=\frac{F(vS)}{F(v)},\qquad
K_v\lvert j\rangle_c
=\frac1{F(v)}\sum_{n=0}^{j}c_nv^n\lvert j-n\rangle_c,
\]
where \(S\) lowers the site label.

Its Fock lift \(\Gamma(K_v)\) applies this transformation to every occupied orbital and antisymmetrizes. It preserves particle number, generally producing a superposition of occupation patterns. Antisymmetrization makes its amplitudes determinants:
\[
\langle I|\Gamma(K_v)|J\rangle
=\det[(K_v)_{i_a j_b}].
\]
For \(I=(0,\ldots,r-1)\) and \(J=(k,\ldots,k+r-1)\), this becomes
\[
\langle I|\Gamma(K_v)|J\rangle
=\frac{v^{rk}}{F(v)^r}D_{r,k}.
\]
That is the transfer operator’s central role: it realizes the coefficient determinants as fermionic transition amplitudes.

To describe its energy, MC08 constructs a Hamiltonian from its activity generator:
\[
G(v)=K'_vK_v^{-1}
=-iH(v)-\tfrac12\mathsf R(v),
\]
\[
H(v)=\frac i2(G-G^\dagger),\qquad
\mathsf R(v)=-(G+G^\dagger).
\]
On the established interval \(0\le v\le1/25\), \(\mathsf R\ge0\). The Fock energy observable is
\[
\mathbb H_{\mathrm{MC08}}(v)=d\Gamma(H(v)).
\]
The Hamiltonian supplies coherent mixing; the loss term supplies attenuation when conditioning on no detected loss. Together they generate \(\Gamma(K_v)\). Actual loss events remove particles. Here \(v\) is the chosen evolution clock, distinct from inverse temperature \(\beta\).

**Coefficient-site occupations generally are not energy eigenstates of this Hamiltonian.** To obtain definite instantaneous energies at a finite cutoff, diagonalize \(H(v)\), then add the eigenvalues of the occupied eigenmodes.

There is a revealing example. In the finite two-site model, at \(v=0\), put \(\alpha=c_1/c_0>0\). Then
\[
H_1(0)=\frac{\alpha}{2}
\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\-i&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its energy eigenstates are
\[
\frac{\lvert0\rangle_c-i\lvert1\rangle_c}{\sqrt2}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac{\lvert0\rangle_c+i\lvert1\rangle_c}{\sqrt2},
\]
with energies \(+\alpha/2\) and \(-\alpha/2\). Each individual site state has **zero mean energy**, but a measurement can yield either energy. More generally, the manuscript’s real coefficient convention makes \(H(v)\) have zero diagonal, so every coefficient occupation basis state has zero mean energy. This does not make them zero-energy eigenstates.

Finally, the original continuum orbitals \(f_i=\Phi^{(2i)}/\sqrt\Phi\) have derivative labels. Each \(f_i\) averages a particular response observable over the entire filtered theta spectrum. Thus the manuscript connects the descriptions through
\[
\text{theta energies}\longrightarrow\Phi
\longrightarrow c_n
\longrightarrow K_v
\longrightarrow\text{fermionic amplitudes}.
\]
It does not identify the energy-mode creators \(b_m^\dagger\) with the coefficient-site creators \(a_j^\dagger\).

Saved in the new [brainstorm note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/brainstorm/notes/01_FOCK_ENERGIES_AND_THETA_TRANSFER_20261102.md), with this chat registered under [brainstorm/chat-histories](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/brainstorm/chat-histories/README.md).
I think we might have to go back to the drawing board on the selection of the Hamiltonian from MC08. Can you explain in detail what motivated that definition?

I’ll trace how MC08 arrived at that Hamiltonian and separate what was fixed by the transfer operator from what was chosen in the physical model. That should clarify what we could change in a redesign.

The original records show that MC08 worked backward from the required transfer \(K_v\). Once it fixed that transfer, the clock \(v\), and the “no detected loss” interpretation, the formula for \(H\) followed uniquely. The main choices to reconsider are those earlier modeling decisions; the later architecture decision chiefly selected how to realize the loss on Fock space.

The clearest motivation appears at \(v=0\): the Hamiltonian produces hopping in both directions, while the loss term cancels one direction, leaving exactly the prescribed backward transfer. This shows why the formula works—and why its spectrum was a consequence of matching the transfer, rather than a starting assumption about theta energy.

MC08’s Hamiltonian came from **working backward from a prescribed transfer operator**. The objective was to construct a physical open-system evolution whose amplitude, conditioned on no detected loss, reproduces that transfer exactly.

That distinction matters for your proposed reconsideration: **the formula for \(H\) is forced within the chosen construction; the earlier decision to use that construction is open to reconsideration.**

The original starting point was
\[
K_v=\frac{F(vS)}{F(v)},
\]
where \(F\) contains the theta coefficients and \(S\) is the backward shift on coefficient sites. This operator was attractive because its fermionic amplitudes reproduce the coefficient minors:
\[
\langle I|\Gamma(K_v)|J\rangle
=
\frac{v^{\sum J-\sum I}}{F(v)^r}
\det[c_{j_b-i_a}].
\]
Thus one operator handles every particle number and every finite minor, with the original signs retained. The normalization by \(F(v)\) makes it a contraction.

The first priority was therefore **preserving this exact mathematical encoding**. An energy spectrum was not supplied as an independent physical input.

The next choice was to regard the activity \(v\) as an evolution clock. Originally, \(v\) weights how far the transfer moves a coefficient-site label. It is distinct from the theta inverse temperature \(\beta=e^{4u}\). Turning it into a clock was an additional modeling decision.

Once we demand
\[
\psi(v)=K_v\psi(0),
\]
the generator is determined wherever \(K_v\) is invertible:
\[
\psi'(v)=G(v)\psi(v),\qquad
G(v)=K'_vK_v^{-1}.
\]
For this transfer,
\[
G(v)=SF'(vS)F(vS)^{-1}
-\frac{F'(v)}{F(v)}I.
\]
At this stage there is still no separately chosen Hamiltonian. We have the generator of a specified operator path.

Because \(K_v\) is generally nonunitary, it cannot directly describe closed-system real-time evolution on the same Hilbert space. MC08 instead interpreted it as the evolution **conditioned on observing no loss into an environment**.

In the usual quantum-jump description, an unnormalized no-count state obeys
\[
\psi'
=
\left(-iH-\frac12\sum_\mu L_\mu^\dagger L_\mu\right)\psi,
\]
with \(\hbar=1\). The \(L_\mu\) describe possible detected events. Their associated attenuation accounts for the decreasing probability that no event has occurred. This is the convention used in [Castin–Dalibard–Mølmer, equations (4)–(11)](https://arxiv.org/html/0805.4002v1).

We can derive the required splitting directly. During a short interval \(\delta v\), write the no-count operator as
\[
M_0=I+G\,\delta v+o(\delta v),
\]
and the count operators to leading order as
\[
M_\mu=\sqrt{\delta v}\,L_\mu.
\]
The probabilities of all possible outcomes must sum to one, so
\[
M_0^\dagger M_0+\sum_\mu M_\mu^\dagger M_\mu
=I+o(\delta v).
\]
Comparing the first-order terms gives
\[
G+G^\dagger+\sum_\mu L_\mu^\dagger L_\mu=0.
\]
Consequently the total loss operator must be
\[
R:=\sum_\mu L_\mu^\dagger L_\mu
=-(G+G^\dagger).
\]

What remains is the anti-Hermitian, norm-preserving part of \(G\). In the Schrödinger convention, that part is \(-iH\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{
H=\frac{i}{2}(G-G^\dagger),\qquad
G=-iH-\frac12R.
}
\]

**This is the precise motivation for the definition.** The factor \(i\) converts the anti-Hermitian generator of coherent motion into a Hermitian Hamiltonian. Equivalently,
\[
H_{\mathrm{eff}}=iG=H-\frac{i}{2}R,
\]
and \(H\) is the Hermitian part of this effective Hamiltonian.

The substantive admissibility question was whether \(R\ge0\). Without that, the algebraic splitting still exists, but it cannot supply nonnegative loss probabilities in this model. MC08-E01 established that positivity on \(0\le v\le1/25\). Merely knowing that each endpoint \(K_v\) is a contraction would not establish the necessary condition at every intermediate time.

The calculation at \(v=0\) shows particularly clearly what this Hamiltonian was designed to do. Put
\[
\alpha=\frac{c_1}{c_0}>0.
\]
Then
\[
G(0)=\alpha(S-I),
\]
and the prescribed splitting gives
\[
H(0)=\frac{i\alpha}{2}(S-S^\dagger),
\qquad
R(0)=\alpha(2I-S-S^\dagger).
\]
Combining them,
\[
\begin{aligned}
-iH(0)-\frac12R(0)
&=\frac{\alpha}{2}(S-S^\dagger)
-\alpha I+\frac{\alpha}{2}(S+S^\dagger)\\
&=\alpha(S-I).
\end{aligned}
\]

The coherent Hamiltonian contains hopping in both directions. The conditional loss term cancels the \(S^\dagger\) contribution, leaving the required directed transfer.

This explains the unusual energy picture from the previous reply. **The Hamiltonian was selected to supply the coherent component of this cancellation.** Its eigenvalues were a consequence of that requirement. The positive discrete-Laplacian expression appears in \(R\), where it controls loss rates.

More generally, writing
\[
\log(F(w)/c_0)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_nw^n,
\]
gives
\[
H(v)=\frac{i}{2}\sum_{n\ge1}
n\lambda_nv^{n-1}\bigl(S^n-(S^\dagger)^n\bigr).
\]
Because the coefficients are real, this has imaginary hopping entries and zero diagonal in the coefficient basis. That accounts for the zero mean energies of the site occupation states.

Zero diagonal entries are compatible with a legitimate Hamiltonian—ordinary hopping models can have this feature. They do, however, show that the site labels were never being assigned the theta energies \(\pi m^2\). All the theta data enter through \(F\), but no correspondence with the circle energy operator was established.

The later [B01 architecture decision](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/notes/02_OPEN_SYSTEM_ARCHITECTURE_DECISION_20261102.md) inherited this \(H\). Its main choice was how to realize the construction on Fock space:
\[
\mathbb H=d\Gamma(H),\qquad
L_\mu=\sum_j(\sqrt R)_{\mu j}a_j.
\]
These linear annihilation operators satisfy
\[
\sum_\mu L_\mu^\dagger L_\mu=d\Gamma(R).
\]
The no-count generator is therefore exactly \(d\Gamma(G)\), and its propagator is \(\Gamma(K_v)\).

This quadratic Hamiltonian and linear loss architecture was useful because it preserves the determinant structure across every particle sector. Fresh vacuum reservoir modes and ideal counting then provide the selected physical realization. The construction did not impose a bath at theta temperature, thermal detailed balance, or conservation of the source energies \(\pi m^2\).

The distinction between choices and consequences is:

| Ingredient | Why it entered |
|---|---|
| Coefficient transfer \(K_v\) | Exact encoding of the original minors |
| Activity \(v\) as clock | Chosen continuous evolution |
| No-count interpretation | Allows a nonunitary amplitude within quantum dynamics |
| \(H=i(G-G^\dagger)/2\) | Forced by that prescribed generator and interpretation |
| Quadratic Hamiltonian and linear losses | Preserve the exterior-power construction across particle sectors |
| Theta energy spectrum | Available from the source, but not used to select this Hamiltonian |

Within the fixed construction, we cannot simply replace \(H\) by an arbitrary preferred energy operator and compensate with different losses. If
\[
0=-i\,\Delta H-\frac12\Delta R,
\]
with both \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta R\) self-adjoint, then both must vanish. This uniqueness fixes the entire phase-calibrated no-count path. Different paths, frames, clock choices, enlarged systems, or measurement arrangements retain design freedom.

My assessment is that **the definition is mathematically well motivated for realizing the chosen transfer, while its suitability as the foundation of an energy-based argument remains a separate question**. If we want the physical reasoning to originate in the square-energy spectrum, I would revisit the earlier decision to make \(K_v\) itself the dynamics. A different approach could start with the circle Hamiltonian and recover the coefficient determinants as observables of that system.

I saved this explanation and the qualifications in [Brainstorm Note02](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/brainstorm/notes/02_HAMILTONIAN_MOTIVATION_AND_DESIGN_CHOICES_20261102.md).

A few points:

- Regarding v as an evolution clock is a choice. At the very least there is the freedom to rescale v. I'm not sure how much that affects the Hamiltonian, but it is probably worth considering that freedom.
- I'd like to understand what the environment is here exactly. I think in order to make progress in this particular case, we will have to specialize some of the open quantum system tools to the case where you have an exact description of the full model, and trace out some of the components. I'm not sure if you've implicitly constructed the external space within the derivation (it could depend on work that I'm not familiar with), but it could be useful to make it more explicit.



We should evaluate these decision points carefully before moving forward, because it seems that a lot of later analysis is inherited from some of these decision points, from what I can tell.

I’ll examine how changing the clock affects the Hamiltonian and losses, then make the environment construction explicit. I’ll also distinguish what is exact in the full model from what is obtained only after a limiting procedure, so we can assess those choices before building on them.

There is an important interaction between these choices. A constant rescaling of \(v\) only rescales the Hamiltonian and loss rates. A clock that starts quadratically, \(v=at^2\), changes the initial loss from linear to quadratic in physical time, so the earlier finite-reservoir obstruction needs that qualification. It still does not automatically give the same continuously monitored loss record.

The existing environment is explicit: a succession of fresh fermion modes, each interacting once with the system. Each finite sequence is a fully specified unitary model; the target MC08 dynamics is recovered in a limit.

I’ve also worked out a concrete comparison with one fixed finite environment. It recovers the exact endpoint amplitudes and admits a regular total Hamiltonian after a quadratic clock start. Its intermediate measurement record differs, which makes the choice between preserving endpoint amplitudes and preserving the whole loss history consequential.

These choices should be evaluated together. **A constant rescaling changes energy and decay-rate scales; a nonlinear clock can also change which full-environment realizations are possible.** The existing environment is explicit, but its exact relationship to the target dynamics involves a limit that deserves careful separation.

There is also a concrete alternative: at every fixed finite mode cutoff, we can construct a single finite environment that reproduces the exact endpoint amplitudes. With a quadratic clock start, that construction has a regular total Hamiltonian. It generally has a different intermediate measurement history.

First, consider the clock. Write
\[
v=f(t),\qquad f(0)=0,\qquad f'(t)\ge0,
\]
and retain the same transfer path:
\[
\widetilde K(t)=K_{f(t)}.
\]
Differentiating gives
\[
\widetilde G(t)=f'(t)G(f(t)).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
\widetilde H(t)=f'(t)H(f(t)),\qquad
\widetilde R(t)=f'(t)R(f(t)),\qquad
\widetilde L_\mu(t)=\sqrt{f'(t)}\,L_\mu(f(t)).
}
\]
The same scaling applies to the Fock Hamiltonian.

For the constant rescaling \(v=at\), this multiplies energies and decay rates by \(a\). At corresponding points along the path, it preserves the energy eigenvectors, the relative strength of coherent evolution and loss, and the determinant amplitudes. Thus it provides a genuine choice of physical timescale, but does not change the underlying Hamiltonian structure or turn its spectrum into \(\pi m^2\).

A clock with \(f'(0)=0\) has a more consequential effect. Previously we used
\[
\|K_v\psi\|^2
=1-v\langle\psi,R(0)\psi\rangle+O(v^2).
\]
This linear initial loss conflicted with a regular total Hamiltonian acting on a system initially independent of a fixed vacuum environment: such a model initially leaks probability only quadratically in physical time.

But if
\[
v=at^2,
\]
then
\[
\|K_{at^2}\psi\|^2
=1-at^2\langle\psi,R(0)\psi\rangle+O(t^4).
\]

**The initial linear-versus-quadratic obstruction disappears.** The earlier obstruction was valid for its chosen clock; it should not be inherited as an exclusion covering this clock change.

That does not settle the entire monitored process. At a later time where \(f'(t)>0\), the prescribed intermediate no-count evolution still has linear loss. Reproducing every intermediate monitored interval is a stronger requirement than reproducing the transfer from the initial time to each endpoint.

The existing MC08 environment can be described quite explicitly. Fix a cutoff with \(m=N+1\) system modes. The system is the fermionic Fock space over those modes. At each step, it encounters **another \(m\) fermion modes, initially empty**:

- The new modes interact with the system once.
- Their outgoing occupation is measured or discarded.
- They never interact with the system again.
- The next step uses another empty collection.

After \(M\) steps, the environment contains \(mM\) modes. All their initial states and interactions are specified.

In combined fermionic notation, the interaction with one collection has the form
\[
W=\sum_\mu
\left(b_\mu^\dagger L_\mu+L_\mu^\dagger b_\mu\right),
\]
where the \(b_\mu\) act on the environment and
\[
L_\mu=\sum_j(\sqrt R)_{\mu j}a_j
\]
acts on the system. This exchanges particles between system and environment. The manuscript includes the parity factors needed to express this correctly in an ordinary tensor-product representation.

For a step of duration \(h\) in the \(v\)-clock, the exact joint unitary is
\[
U_h(v)=
\exp\!\left[-i\left(h\,\mathbb H(v)+\sqrt h\,W(v)\right)\right].
\]
Equivalently, its total Hamiltonian during that step is
\[
\mathbb H(v)+h^{-1/2}W(v).
\]

This gives a completely specified finite joint model. Two different operations on it must remain distinct:
\[
\rho_S'=
\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left[
U_h(\rho_S\otimes|\Omega_E\rangle\langle\Omega_E|)
U_h^\dagger
\right]
\]
is the **unconditioned reduced state**, whereas
\[
M_0=\langle\Omega_E|U_h|\Omega_E\rangle
\]
is the amplitude operator for finding the outgoing environment empty. Keeping every measured occupation gives the full count record.

The exactness levels are:

| Object | What MC08 establishes |
|---|---|
| A finite sequence of these interactions | An explicit, exact joint unitary model |
| Its reduced dynamics at finite step size | An approximation to the target MC08 dynamics |
| Limit as the step size tends to zero, at fixed system cutoff | Convergence to the target channel, count instrument and no-count amplitude |
| One regular infinite-reservoir Hamiltonian generating everything | Not constructed by that convergence proof |

The limit requires increasingly many fresh modes and increasingly strong instantaneous couplings. The subsequent extension to infinitely many **system** modes is a separate result.

Also, these auxiliary environment modes have not been identified with omitted theta energy modes. The construction specifies neither a bath spectrum related to \(\pi m^2\) nor a bath at inverse temperature \(\beta\). It was designed from the desired reduced dynamics.

For comparison, we can make a **fixed finite environment** explicit without taking that collision limit.

At a fixed cutoff, put
\[
C(t)=K_{f(t),N},
\]
and add one copy of the system’s one-particle space as the environment. Define
\[
D(t)=\sqrt{I-C(t)^\dagger C(t)},\qquad
E(t)=\sqrt{I-C(t)C(t)^\dagger}.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
U(t)=
\begin{pmatrix}
C(t)&-E(t)\\
D(t)&C(t)^\dagger
\end{pmatrix}
}
\]
is unitary and satisfies \(U(0)=I\). This uses the standard contraction-completion identity described by [Robinson, Theorems 0–2](https://arxiv.org/html/1803.09329v1).

For one particle initially in the system,
\[
U(t)\binom{\psi}{0}
=
\binom{C(t)\psi}{D(t)\psi}.
\]
We therefore know exactly both the retained system amplitude and the amplitude transferred to the environment.

Taking its fermionic lift gives a unitary on the Fock space of \(m\) system modes plus \(m\) environment modes. With the environment initially empty,
\[
\boxed{
\langle\Omega_E|\Gamma(U(t))|\Omega_E\rangle
=\Gamma(C(t)).
}
\]
Thus final vacuum selection recovers precisely the original determinant amplitudes. Tracing out the environment instead gives an exact reduced channel.

The clock now matters to the regularity of the total Hamiltonian. With \(f(t)=at^2\),
\[
C(t)=I+at^2G_N(0)+O(t^4),
\]
and
\[
D(t)=\sqrt a\,t\sqrt{R_N(0)}+O(t^3),
\]
with the analogous expansion for \(E(t)\). The square-root behavior in \(v\) becomes ordinary linear behavior in \(t\).

At each fixed finite cutoff, this produces a smooth unitary path and a regular, explicitly determined total Hamiltonian
\[
h_{\mathrm{tot}}(t)=i\,\dot U(t)U(t)^\dagger.
\]
Its Fock lift generates the full joint evolution. This is a direct calculation from this discussion, not a result covered by the prior MC08 review. The finite-cutoff qualification matters: this argument does not supply uniform bounds or a regular generator in the infinite-mode limit.

The crucial difference is the measurement history. In a fixed environment, a particle can leave and later return. Finding that environment empty at the final time is therefore different from finding every outgoing collision bin empty.

Indeed, the system block of the fixed-environment propagator between two times is
\[
\bigl[U(t_2)U(t_1)^\dagger\bigr]_{SS}
=
C(t_2)C(t_1)^\dagger+E(t_2)E(t_1).
\]
It is generally different from
\[
C(t_2)C(t_1)^{-1},
\]
the prescribed MC08 intermediate no-count map. Measuring the environment at an intermediate time changes the subsequent conditional evolution.

This gives us a concrete decision to evaluate:

| Requirement | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Recover the original signed amplitudes at observation times | The fixed finite environment is an exact candidate at each cutoff |
| Preserve MC08’s entire continuously monitored loss record | The fixed-environment construction does not automatically suffice |
| Derive energy behavior from the theta spectrum | Neither construction has yet supplied that identification |

My recommendation is to **keep the original determinant amplitudes fixed, while treating the clock, environment and measurement history as design choices**. We should retain the full MC08 count instrument only if it serves the physical relation we want to derive. An exact joint model is a useful starting point for that assessment, but its energy interpretation still needs its own justification.
